+def _apply_table(s, table):
+    """
+    Replace every pair of table in order (same as s = s.replace(ps, c) for all
+    entries), skipping entries that cannot match: a pair occurs only if both of
+    its tokens are in s. present is a superset of the tokens in s (tokens are
+    only ever added: either initially present or minted by a replace that
+    found something), so no replace that would change s is skipped.
+    """
+    present = set(s)
+    add = present.add
+    for ps, c, a, b in table:
+        if a in present and b in present:
+            n = len(s)
+            s = s.replace(ps, c)
+            if len(s) != n:
+                add(c)
+    return s

actions.reason: No change evaluated as an improvement. The first attempt skipped table merges whose tokens were absent. It passed equivalence but made encode_ir 1.14% worse, because most merges do apply. The second evaluate was a throwaway probe that stubs out encoding and training, and it breaks tests and equivalence. It is still in minbpe/regex.py and must not be kept. It showed that only about 19% of train_ir and 21% of encode_ir is controllable library work; the rest is startup, imports and corpus generation. So a 1% gain needs about a 5% speed-up of already heavily optimised code. Possible next steps: keep replace strings one byte wide by mapping merge tokens to byte codes the text doesn't use, or cut per-merge overhead in the regex trainer.
